title: Reduction-Aware Directive-Based Programming via Multi-Dimensional Homomorphisms
problem: Traditional directive-based models (OpenMP, OpenACC) struggle with reduction-intensive computations and fail to deliver consistently portable performance across CPU and GPU architectures.
motivation: Reduction operations are ubiquitous in scientific computing (linear algebra, data mining, quantum chemistry) but are poorly optimized by generic directive frameworks. A specialized abstraction is needed to enable both high performance and programmer productivity.
method: The approach introduces new programming directives (annotations developers add to guide optimization) specifically built for tensor computations with many reductions—operations where values across multi-dimensional arrays get combined repeatedly into fewer results. These directives are grounded in Multi-Dimensional Homomorphisms (MDH), a mathematical framework that preserves structural properties through transformations, and designed for data-parallel operations (calculations running in parallel on many data elements). The implementation is a Python-based framework that compiles code for both CPUs and GPUs using OMPCCL (a portable library managing collective communication between processors), ensuring the same code runs efficiently on either hardware without requiring manual optimization.
key_novelty: The innovation applies Multi-Dimensional Homomorphisms—a mathematical framework that preserves structural properties—to directive design, enabling efficient reduction-heavy tensor computations with portable performance across CPUs and GPUs.
contributions: MDH-based directive specification for data-parallel tensor computations
Portable performance across CPUs (Intel MKL/oneMKL) and GPUs (NVIDIA cuBLAS/cuDNN)
5x speedups on CPUs and 2x on GPUs vs. vendor libraries
Python language integration for enhanced programmer productivity
limitations: Performance claims against vendor libraries may not account for all optimization techniques; specific hardware generations tested not detailed in abstract; generalization to non-reduction operations unclear.
